extracted.intended_audience: Members of the public, advocates, attorneys, or organizations who want to propose or comment on OATH rules
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for proposing, commenting on, and submitting rulemaking petitions to the NYC Office of Administrative Trials and Hearings (OATH), including procedural requirements, publication practices, and submission methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance with the City Administrative Procedure Act (CAPA)
rubrics_metrics.description: OATH proposes and adopts rules in accordance with the City Administrative Procedure Act (CAPA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rulemaking activity (proposed and final rules, hearings, comments) must follow CAPA procedures; OATH conducts publication, hearings, and comment processes under that statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication of proposed and final rules
rubrics_metrics.description: OATH publishes its proposed and final rules in The City Record and NYC Rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed and final rules will appear in both The City Record (the City's newspaper for public hearings and meetings, proposed and adopted rules, and other notifications) and the NYC Rules portal so the public can find and review them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public hearings and acceptance of comments
rubrics_metrics.description: OATH holds public hearings and accepts comments from the public on proposed rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For each proposed rule OATH may hold a public hearing; transcripts of hearings and written comments are made available (see linked transcripts). The page directs readers to links for how to attend a hearing and submit comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: New Rule Petition content requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: If you would like to propose a new rule to OATH, you can submit a typewritten petition. The petition should include: the proposed rule and all suggested language of the rule that you would like OATH to consider; your argument in support of the rule; you or your authorized representative’s name, telephone number, mailing address, and email address; and your or your authorized representative’s signature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitions must be typewritten and include full suggested text, a supporting argument, contact information for the petitioner or authorized representative, and a signature. This is the minimum information OATH requests for considering a new-rule petition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ways to submit a petition
rubrics_metrics.description: Submission methods: Email: Rules_Oath@oath.nyc.gov; Mail or In-Person: Office of Administrative Trials and Hearings, 66 John Street, 11th Floor, New York, NY 10038, ATTN: General Counsel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OATH accepts petitions by email, mail, or in-person delivery. Include ATTN: General Counsel for mailed/in-person submissions. Ensure petition complies with content requirements when submitting by any method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules for submission and processing of rulemaking petitions (procedural reference)
rubrics_metrics.description: For more information about OATH's current Proposed Rules and recent Final Rules, or on how to attend a public hearing and submit a comment on a proposed rule, click on the relevant links below.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page points to additional procedural materials ('Rules for Submission and Processing of Rulemaking Petitions' and links for Proposed Rules and Final Rules) that provide further instructions and processing details; users should consult those resources for timelines, processing steps, and any additional requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transcript and record availability for rulemakings
rubrics_metrics.description: Transcripts of public hearings and written comments are referenced for each proposed/final rule (e.g., 'Read the transcript of the February 22, 2023 Public Hearing on this rule and written comments').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OATH posts hearing transcripts and written comments associated with proposed and final rules, enabling review of the record that informed rulemaking. Users can consult those transcripts to see the discussion and comments received during the rulemaking process.
